title: Labour: Don't change course; help to turbo-charge it.
author: Sherrington, Tom
summary: Written in direct response to England's new Education Secretary's tepid, credit-avoidant reaction to strong PISA 2025 results, this piece argues the political left is making a strategic and pedagogical mistake by distancing itself from a curriculum-behaviour-instruction agenda that the evidence now shows is working, purely to avoid appearing to credit the previous government's reforms. The author, an influential voice in the English 'traditionalist' education movement, argues the emerging cross-political consensus around a knowledge-rich curriculum, strong behaviour systems, and instructional teaching should be seen as a genuine, evidence-backed achievement worth sustaining rather than reversing, and drafts the alternative statement he believes the Education Secretary should have made, one that credits the system's progress while still opening space for legitimate new priorities like oracy and technical education pathways. The piece explicitly frames continued refinement (adding oracy, rebalancing toward the arts, addressing GCSE overload) as compatible with, not opposed to, the existing agenda, closing with a direct appeal against 'playing party politics' with education policy at a moment the author believes represents genuine, hard-won progress.
points: The piece argues the political left is making a strategic error by distancing itself from a curriculum-behaviour-instruction agenda that PISA 2025 data now shows is working, purely to avoid crediting the previous government's reforms.

The author drafts an alternative statement he believes the Education Secretary should have made — one crediting the system's progress on curriculum, instructional teaching, and behaviour while still opening space for new priorities.

A specific historical parallel is drawn to David Miliband's 'personalised learning' agenda in the 2000s, described as '90% wishful rhetoric; 10% practicalities,' as a cautionary precedent for vague progressive alternatives.

New priorities like strengthening oracy and widening technical/vocational pathways are explicitly framed as compatible refinements within the existing agenda, not a change of direction requiring abandoning it.

The piece closes with a direct political appeal: 'this isn't the time to play party politics' with an education agenda the author believes represents genuine, hard-won, evidence-backed progress that is only 'half way up the mountain.'
quotes: The left in general - needs to embrace and strengthen the current curriculum, behaviour, instruction agenda. These are our best bets by far. But ideological dogma stands in the way.

Powell has, to me, seemed out of touch with the depth of thinking and dynamic work going on across the system: the discourse around curriculum, evidence-informed practices and the design of behaviour systems.

When you see as many lessons as I do around the place it is so obvious that there are huge gaps to close in terms of curriculum, behaviour and instructional teaching and these are the ways to secure deeper learning for more children.

The curriculum has been stable enough, the teaching and learning agenda sustained enough and the discourse around behaviour coherent enough for a consensus to have emerged that is starting to pay dividends.
We're only half way up the mountain. We can see the path ahead. It's not easy but it's clear. This is not the time so protest that we're climbing the wrong mountain.
This isn't the time to play party politics. Let's not lose focus; let's double down and get right up that mountain.
